item.title: Battle of Chile director Patricio Guzmán dies aged 85
item.description:
Passionate documentary maker won international acclaim for unsparing but poetic films exploring the impact of the Pinochet regime in Chile

Patricio Guzmán, the film-maker who chronicled Chile’s bloody 1970s political strife and its subsequent social and political turmoil in films such as The Battle of Chile and Nostalgia for the Light, has died aged 85. According to Chilean news outlet Emol, Guzmán died on Tuesday in Paris after a cardiorespiratory arrest.

Guzmán’s chief preoccupation throughout his career was the carnage unleashed by Augusto Pinochet’s coup in 1973 against Salvador Allende, Chile’s elected president. He later told the Guardian: “I’m a film-maker who was very marked by the ways of the dictator. It has remained with me for ever. I cannot leave it behind.” However, he resisted the idea that he was an activist, political film-maker, adding: “I’m not a sociologist. Neither am I a politician. I make films that are metaphorical and poetic; I interpret reality through my own personal way of looking.”

item.title: Thick smoke seen near Riyadh airport as Houthis claim attack on Saudi capital
item.description:
Authorities issued warnings for city in first such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with Iran-backed Houthis escalated in July

Yemen’s Houthis said they attacked “sensitive” sites in the Saudi capital with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of black smoke were seen rising above Riyadh airport on Saturday.

The Saudi government sent air raid alerts to citizens by phone overnight warning of aerial attacks, marking the first time the government has issued such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis escalated in July.

item.title: Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces launch inquest into sudden military collapse
item.description:
Rout raises questions about coordination and morale as some politicians claim billions of dollars were offered to persuade forces to abandon position

A bitter inquest is under way among Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces as to how what was being billed as a decisive assault on Sana’a, the Houthi-controlled capital, suddenly collapsed into a military rout.

More than 15 brigades were defeated as the country’s entire west coast fell into Houthi hands. Efforts are now being made to reorganise the anti-Houthi forces representing the UN-recognised Yemeni government in order to capture the Kahbob mountains, a strategic point from which to restrict Houthi forces moving closer to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait.

item.title: Turkish foreign minister says Israel should not 'chase empty dreams'
item.description:
Turkish foreign minister says Israel should not 'chase empty dreams'

Turkish Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus has accused Israel of seeking to deepen divisions across the Middle East in its pursuit for a 'promised land'.

“Israel should not chase empty dreams,” Kurtulmus said during a civil society gathering in Kirsehir, according to Al Jazeera.

“Israel’s main goal is for the peoples of this region to fall out with each other, to fight each other, and to realise its own ‘promised land’,” he added.

However, he said, Turkey "will bring this region together and continue on our path".

Kurtulmus said Israel had carried out attacks in recent years against Palestine, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Yemen and Qatar, arguing that almost every country in the region had been affected by conflict.

“They want to divide and fragment; we want to unite and integrate,” Kurtulmus said. “They want to scatter; we want to bring people together.”

item.title: 'Middle East situation could escalate rapidly': US urges citizens to exercise caution
item.description:
'Middle East situation could escalate rapidly': US urges citizens to exercise caution

The US government has told its citizens currently in the Middle East that the security environment remains "complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation", urging them to  exercise heightened vigilance.

In a statement, the state department asked Americans to also be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions.

In separate travel alerts for Iraq, Bahrain, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Iran, Qatar, Lebanon, Kuwait and Jordan, US diplomatic missions in the nine countries said the security environment in the Middle East poses “the risk of flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions as regional tensions rise”.

"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports. This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly. Americans outside the Middle East should seriously reconsider travel to and through the region," the alert said.

The alerts warned that Iran and groups supportive of Tehran could target US interests overseas or locations associated with Americans.

US citizens were advised to monitor airline and airport operations, avoid demonstrations and large gatherings and follow instructions from local authorities.

item.title: Iran disputes US oil claim, approves new rule on Hormuz data cables
item.description:
Iran disputes US oil claim, approves new rule on Hormuz data cables

Iran has disputed a claim by US Central Command (Centcom) that it escorted tankers carrying more than a billion barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

Armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi called the claim a “failed psychological operation” meant to boost US troop morale and justify the war’s financial and human costs, Iran’s Fars news agency reported.

Centcom had also said it protected more than 2,000 commercial transits through the strait and cleared its main shipping lanes of mines, in addition to facilitating oil exports.

Separately, a committee of senior Iranian officials has approved a rule requiring Tehran’s approval for data cables routed through the strait, Fars reported.

The measure, known as Article 10, will also apply to other data communications equipment passing through the waterway, with further details to be set out in upcoming regulations.

item.title: Houthi missiles on Riyadh and other cities intercepted, Saudi coalition says
item.description:
Houthi missiles on Riyadh and other cities intercepted, Saudi coalition says

Saudi-led coalition forces said air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by Houthis toward Riyadh at dawn on Saturday, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said in a statement.

Saudi Arabia's air force "successfully intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthi terrorist militia," al-Maliki posted on X.

He said the Houthis also tried to target "civilians and civilian infrastructure in Bisha, Taif, Farasan, and Yanbu," adding that the attacks "were thwarted by the Gulf monarchy's air defences".

Al-Maliki accused the Houthis of escalating such attempts and affirmed the coalition's right to take "appropriate measures" against the group under international humanitarian law.

item.title: Houthis claim strikes on Riyadh, Yanbu while Saudi coalition says attacks thwarted
item.description:
Houthis claim strikes on Riyadh, Yanbu while Saudi coalition says attacks thwarted

Submitted by Ayse Betul Aytekin on Sat, 09/19/2026 - 21:14
Air defences intercepted Houthi missiles before they reached Riyadh, the coalition said, in attacks Turkey warned should not draw Saudi Arabia into the US-Iran war.
Large plume of black smoke rises from the fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, 19 September 2026 (Reuters)
Off

Saudi-led coalition forces say air defences intercepted a Houthi missile fired at Riyadh, hours after the group claimed the strikes.

Riyadh came under missile and drone fire on Saturday, according to Yemen's Houthis, who claimed responsibility for strikes on what they called "sensitive" sites in the Saudi capital and on Aramco facilities in the coastal city of Yanbu.

Coalition spokesperson, Major General Turki al-Maliki, said air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired at Riyadh, and thwarted separate attempts to target Taif, Baish, Farasan, and Yanbu before they reached their targets.

He accused the Houthis of escalating efforts to target civilians and civilian infrastructure, and said the coalition reserves the right to take "appropriate measures" against the group under international humanitarian law.

Saudi authorities had issued an early-morning alert telling residents to shelter indoors, the first such warning in this latest round of fighting with the Houthis.

Hours later, several people in Riyadh told AFP they heard a series of explosions echo across the city.

Around the same time, firefighters extinguished a blaze at a fuel depot near Riyadh's airport, where a tanker bearing the Aramco logo had caught fire. Footage circulating online showed smoke rising nearby.

It was not immediately clear whether the airport fire was connected to the reported strikes.

Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement that the strikes were "in response to the Saudi enemy's criminal attempts to target the capital Sanaa," confirming that Houthi forces had hit targets in both Riyadh and Yanbu using a mix of missiles and drones.

Limited support from allies

The attacks come amid rapid Houthi territorial gains in recent weeks, which have left Yemen's Saudi-backed government on the back foot despite a sustained Saudi air campaign against Houthi-held areas.

Days earlier, Saudi officials had accused the Houthi group of attempting to strike Mecca, calling it a "cowardly terrorist attack" on the city that draws millions of Muslim pilgrims each year. The Houthis rejected the claim as false.

The group says it faces near-constant Saudi bombardment as it pushes to seize full control of Yemen's Red Sea coastline, a campaign that would hand it the Bab al-Mandab strait, a major global shipping route.

The kingdom's recently signed defence pacts with Turkey and Pakistan have done little to counter the growing Houthi threat.

Later on Saturday, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan condemned the reported attacks on Saudi territory and oil infrastructure, saying the kingdom should be "kept out" of the broader conflict between Iran and the United States.

He also added that Saudi Arabia may have military needs due to the ongoing Houthi attacks and that Turkey was ready to help under the trilateral defence pact.

Pakistan has said that there were no discussions about a military reaction from Islamabad under the Mecca agreement in response to the Houthis' attacks, but added that they would act when the "time comes".

The US, on the other hand, has been offering the kingdom only limited support of its own, as the American news outlet Axios reported last week that Washington turned down a Saudi request to strike the Houthis directly.

Still, on Thursday, the US approved a $24.3 billion sale of F-35 fighter jets to the kingdom, saying the deal would help Riyadh "deter current and future threats," according to the State Department.

The war in Yemen began in 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and other regions, leading to a Saudi-led intervention in March 2015.

A fragile 2022 truce held for years before collapsing in July, after the Houthis defied Saudi control of Yemeni airspace by allowing an Iranian aircraft to land in the country.

The Houthis' recent seizure of Yemen's coastline has raised widespread international concern, adding to disruption in global maritime trade already caused by Iran's blockade of Hormuz.

The group insists shipping in the sea lane faces no threat, except for vessels linked to Saudi Arabia.

Facing limited outside backing, Saudi Arabia has been putting in an effort to expand its own military role in Yemen.

item.title: Turkey says it will look into Saudi military needs as part of defence pact
item.description:
Turkey says it will look into Saudi military needs as part of defence pact

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Saturday that Saudi Arabia may have some military needs due to the ongoing attacks by Yemen's Houthis and that Turkey would look into them as part of a trilateral defence pact signed with Pakistan.

Speaking on broadcaster NTV, Fidan said it was unacceptable for Saudi Arabia to be made a part of the US-Iran war, as it had no desire to join the conflict, and added without elaborating, that proposals have been conveyed to all sides to end the fighting.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Joint Defence Agreement in August in Mecca, under which an attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all.
